\CRchapter{18}{The Turning into Seed}{Days 85–90 · Silt 26–30, Seed 1, Y.H. 813}{Low Kiln, Sill}
\CRepigraph{Silt goes out on mud and Seed comes in on the same ground. Move the loaves along the shelf; the space at the end has not moved. A month is a vessel turned, and what was left in it is still in it.}{A proverb of the kiln yards, Sill}

\begin{CRchronicle}{18}
Silt went out on the mud it had come in on. The yard swept around what the water left and entered none of it --- the brown skin holding a boot’s print, the clean dark line, the finer grey called the thaw, the space under the rack. Sella Vail carried the boy at the half-pace from every open slate to his bed. The house kept its days in loaves and glances and a place nobody would call a number; the boy kept his count exactly and could spend none.

Tarn set his knife on its sill and told the empty yard where it was, six years worn flat by his thumb, the seventh nearly gone and still held. \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count}, he told the kindling, wanting the late thaw because it puts off the paying; his broom went over the collector’s road without turning. Jorra Vail came in with grey slate dust past his bent finger, told a pot it would do and moved the damper ahead of Sella’s sentence; he did not look toward the bed.

Three doors down the pewter tin above the empty bed kept its pale fold. Alda Reed laid her birth-slates on the bench before she turned to the fold, pressed the wool a breath too long, crossed two fingers at the birth-flower before she knew it and covered the sign with the date of a woman more mornings dead than any living person kept count of. \emph{Warm and breathing, that’s all I’ve set down}, she said, exact and not true. Her hand went once to the tin in her bodice without opening it; her sixth slate lay face-down.

At the Fishstairs Mira Silt answered a question with her own --- \emph{It comes when it comes. Ask the river}. When a buyer named a figure her thumb went to the grey cord, showing the second twisted twice beneath it, neither knot counted. The steps came back four, four and a landing out of line that a market walked carefully over. On the last market Berr Clay wiped his thumb twice, read one in twelve and said, \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me}; the true subtraction went unspoken and the number for the thaw arrived nowhere. A foundling turned his head toward a pot a half-beat after the boy’s and could not say why.

Seed opened on mud and the first work of it was sweeping. The carried fire kept four, four and a gap under blind ash; one crust lay stiff in the fold and the empty place beside it crossed into Seed without a name. At dusk Sella put the fold right and left the thread at his mouth frozen, the river’s note and the fire’s gap in two places as for ninety days. He was ninety days old and nobody had told him so. His hand went up an inch toward the water and came down. Nothing had been joined, paid, explained or ended.
\end{CRchronicle}
